Lessons.Title: Times as Many
ExplanationParagraphs:
Learning goal: You will interpret and represent multiplicative comparison situations using objects and diagrams.
In previous grades, you learned how to represent additive comparison situations using discrete diagrams, tape diagrams, and addition and subtraction equations that use symbols to represent an unknown quantity. You used these representations to find differences. In this lesson, you interpret the language of “times as many” in multiplicative comparison situations and connect this language to representations.
Core relationship: Multiplicative comparison means equal groups. If one amount is k times as many as another, multiply the comparison base amount by k.

Local publisher 2021 source lesson activities: Warm-up:  Notice and Wonder: Compare Cubes	 (10 minutes); Activity 1:  Twice as Many	 (10 minutes); Activity 2:  Times as Many	 (20 minutes); Activity 3:  Make $n$ Times as Many	 [OPTIONAL] (15 minutes); Cool-down:  Three Times as Many Cubes	 (5 minutes)
Source-aligned Edulytics model: Andre has 3 cubes and Han has 8 times as many. How many does Han have?
First-party Cool-down (not gated original): Show six times as many as four cubes using a tape diagram.
Original visual/physical and peer-explanation activities still require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiplicative comparison means equal groups
KeyConcepts.Rule: If one amount is k times as many as another, multiply the comparison base amount by k.
KeyConcepts.Example: Andre has 3 cubes and Han has 8 times as many. How many does Han have?

KeyConcepts.Title: Lesson mathematical relationship
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplicative comparison means one quantity is a specified number of times another.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiplicative comparison means one quantity is a specified number of times another.
KeyConcepts.Example: Maya has 7 counters; Leo has four times as many. How many?

KeyConcepts.Title: Independent verification
KeyConcepts.Definition: A tape diagram has a repeated equal unit, not just a fixed additive difference.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A tape diagram has a repeated equal unit, not just a fixed additive difference.
KeyConcepts.Example: A length of 6 cm is tripled. What is the new length?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating 'eight times' as adding eight cubes.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It changes the unit, place value, or operation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: If one amount is k times as many as another, multiply the comparison base amount by k.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Interpreting four times as many as four more.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The mathematical operation or unit interpretation is incorrect.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Four times seven is 28, whereas seven plus four is 11.
